newsitem.title: JAPAN: Second attack on Iraq jars Japan markets.
newsitem.headline: Second attack on Iraq jars Japan markets.

text.p: Japanese stock and oil markets were shaken on Wednesday by a second U.S. missile attack on Iraq.
But the dollar, which rose against the yen after Tuesday's attack, showed little reaction on Japanese markets, refusing to stray far from the 109.25/30 level.
Crude oil futures prices in Asia, however, jumped 30 cents a barrel in the minutes after the initial report that the United States had launched the second attack.
Stockbrokers said they were surprised as the market had thought Tuesday's attack was a one-off incident.

"Wall Street as well as Tokyo thought that the fiasco was over, just part of President Clinton's election campaign and anxiety was fading when the second round came," said Keiji Arai, a strategist at Sanyo Securities.

The key Nikkei was down at the end of the morning session by 30.24 points, or 0.15 percent, at 20,167.91 after rising slightly at the open. But shortly before the break, it fell as low as 20,066.02, startled by the renewed U.S. attacks.

U.S. administration officials said the U.S. military launched a second cruise missile attack on Iraq. The officials said 17 missiles were fired from four ships in a "mop-up" operation authorised by President Bill Clinton.
The second wave was aimed at military targets in southern Iraq not destroyed in an attack by 27 missiles on Tuesday.
Stock market sources expect the impact to be fairly limited as currencies were little affected by the missile attack.
"The yen/dollar rate is not responding to the news," Arai said. "The markets may need some more time to assess the impact."
Koji Asano, a senior manager at Fuji Bank, said: "We don't see the typical 'dollar buying in a crisis' because it isn't a crisis."

The prompt New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) October light crude futures contract, trading in Asia on the ACCESS screen system, jumped to $23.65 per barrel from the $23.35 it was at before the report.

Tsutomu Toichi, director of the Institute of Energy Economics in Tokyo, said: "I don't think NYMEX light crude will rise as high as $30 unless there is a major escalation in the confrontation. But it could top the high of yesterday."

And the October Brent crude contract, trading on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), rose as high as $22.50 per barrel after the news on Wednesday, up 29 cents from the London close.

One broker said the latest escalation of hostilities could push the October Brent contract to match its day-earlier high of $23.50, which was also the highest for any prompt month Brent contract since the Gulf War of 1991.
But he said he expected traders to be cautious about over-reacting. "I don't think there will be as much panic today as yesterday."
Japanese government bonds and Euroyen interest rate futures also dipped slightly on the news of the second attack. However, there was no reaction in trading of the key U.S. 30-year treasury bond.
